title: Buddha-nature
hookLine: all beings have the nature of Buddha, covered but never lost

cards: A lump of gold slips out of someone's hand and falls into a pit of filth. Years go by. From the edge there's nothing to see but muck.
And still the gold hasn't rusted, or shrunk, or turned into muck. It's simply covered. Then someone who can see through the mess points: there's gold down there.
Dig it out and wash it. That picture comes from a Mahayana sutra, and it isn't really about gold. It's about every living being.

teach.b: You met Buddha-nature last year, with Chinul. Today, where it comes from. First, the claim.
Some Mahayana sutras teach that every living being carries the nature of a Buddha. Greed, anger and confusion cover it, but never destroy it.
One sutra is named for the idea, the Tathagatagarbha, often given in English as the womb, or the embryo, of the Buddha. Second, the pictures. That sutra shows more than it argues.
Gold in filth. Honey hidden in a swarm of bees. A grain inside its husk.

teach.h: GOLD, HONEY, A STATUE IN RAGS.
teach.b: A precious statue of the Buddha, wrapped in dirty rags and left by the road, where people walk right past it. Same shape every time: something valuable, something covering it, and the covering is not the thing.
Third, the question. Buddhists read this more than one way. Some hear a seed, a potential for awakening that practice helps grow.
Others, in some Zen and Tibetan teaching, hear it as already whole, like the sun behind clouds: practice doesn't make it, practice uncovers it.

And the Pali texts that Theravada Buddhists keep don't teach Buddha-nature; their line is that the mind is bright, and stained by what visits it. Each reading is held in good faith. Fourth, the hard part.
If it's true, it's true of everyone, including the coworker who talks over people and the relative who knows exactly which button to press.

teach.h: THE RAGS ARE NOT THE STATUE.
teach.b: The people walking past the statue aren't wicked. They just can't see past the rags. Greed and anger do real harm.
They just aren't the whole story of a person.

how: Mahayana teachers in East Asia and Tibet speak of Buddha-nature when they explain why awakening is possible for anyone; some Zen teachers describe sitting itself as an expression of it.

o: a calm temperament some people are lucky to be born with
the goodness a person slowly earns over many lifetimes
the nature of a Buddha in every being, covered but never lost

games.q: covered, not lost: tap the pairs.
p: walked past by people on the road
one reading: a potential that grows

s: Buddha-nature means some beings are born better than others
the teaching says every being has it, covered but never lost.
Buddhists all read Buddha-nature the same way
some hear a seed that grows, some hear something already whole, and the Pali texts don't teach it at all.
in the sutra's picture, the gold stays gold in the filth
it hasn't rusted or shrunk. it's only covered.

games.q: you're on a road, and you pass a bundle of dirty rags. under them, the sutra says, is a precious statue of the Buddha. what do the people on the road do?
o: unwrap it and carry it to a shrine
walk right past it, seeing only rags
games.why: in the picture, people pass it by. they aren't wicked; they just can't see past the covering. that's the point of the image.

practice: Bring to mind one person you find difficult, not the hardest one, someone in the middle, and notice whatever tightens in your chest or jaw.
Without excusing anything they've done, picture the rags, the habits, the fear, the sharp edges, and allow that something else might be under them, the way gold is under the muck.
You don't need to see it; just leave room for it, and if it gets to be too much, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Buddha-nature. The teaching that every being has the nature of a Buddha, covered by greed, anger and confusion, but never lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the sutra and the teaching, often given in English as the womb or embryo of the Buddha.

carryVoice: Your line: covered, not lost. Gold stays gold, even in the muck. Tomorrow, three bodies.

sources.ref: Tathagatagarbha Sutra, the similes (gold in filth, honey among bees, grain in the husk, the statue in rags)
Mahayana Mahaparinirvana Sutra, on all beings having Buddha-nature
